frameworks.name: Three Wheels of Revenue
frameworks.definition: Service businesses generate revenue from three distinct sources: equipment/core product sales, consumable supplies, and service offerings around the core product.

frameworks.name: Customer LTV Extension Strategy
frameworks.definition: A two-step approach to increasing customer lifetime value: first establish high retention on consumables and service (90-95% annual retention), then target higher-tier customers who buy in greater volume.

claims.text: A duct cleaning supply distributor operating at $1.2M revenue with only word-of-mouth customer acquisition has demand capacity but lacks the acquisition systems to reach those customers; the business has mastered product quality but lacks the sales and marketing infrastructure that characterizes mature distribution companies.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Word-of-mouth businesses become capacity-bound by definition because referral networks grow linearly while structured acquisition systems compound.
bounded_by: Requires documented product quality and customer satisfaction

claims.text: For equipment supply businesses, the acquisition method (outbound, paid ads, affiliate, or content) matters less than selection consistency; the constraint is choosing one method and executing at volume rather than dabbling across all four.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: scaling from founder-dependent to systematized acquisition
claims.mechanism: Each acquisition channel requires distinct operational systems and skill development; switching between channels prevents mastery and volume scaling.
bounded_by: Does not apply to platforms with diverse audience (consumer retail, marketplace)
Assumes founder has capacity to execute chosen channel

claims.text: Service businesses structured around equipment sales (printers, auto parts, duct cleaning supplies) work across three independent revenue levers: equipment/core product sales, consumable supplies (high margin), and service offerings, with the economic viability of the business depending on whether consumables and service can achieve high retention and high margin rather than on equipment sales volume.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Consumables and service create recurring revenue moats; selling equipment at cost or low margin is economically rational when consumable margins are 60-80%, because the installed base generates annuity revenue over customer lifetime.
bounded_by: Does not apply to pure product businesses without service or consumable components
Assumes consumables are bought regularly by same customer pool

claims.text: For a duct cleaning supply business averaging 80 new customers monthly with low repeat-customer ratio, the path to revenue growth from $1.2M to $3.5M is to first establish 90-95% annual retention on consumables (creating an annuity base), then later pursue higher-tier customers who buy in greater volume, rather than attempting to increase per-customer spend on low-margin consumables.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B equipment supply with low repeat rate
claims.mechanism: Retention on consumables creates predictable annuity revenue as the customer base grows; higher-tier customer targeting requires different sales motion and channel but can 5-10x customer volume and consumable spend without changing the core product.
bounded_by: Requires establishing predictable consumable ordering cadence

claims.text: A business owner claiming cluelessness about growth challenges but operating profitably at $1.2M revenue with product-market fit is actually ahead of most businesses; the hard part (product quality, customer willingness to buy, profitability) is solved, and the remaining work is systematic customer acquisition and offer design.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: strong product quality validated by word-of-mouth
growth blocked by acquisition, not product
claims.mechanism: Profitability and word-of-mouth traction signal that product-market fit exists; the psychological perception of complexity prevents founders from recognizing how much structural work is already complete.
bounded_by: Only applies when profitability and customer acquisition capability are both present
Does not apply to businesses with product or market fit problems

claims.text: The highest-leverage next step for a supply business with 80 new customers monthly and no outbound to existing customers is to implement a re-engagement and subscription cadence with that 80-customer monthly base, converting them from one-time buyers to recurring consumable subscribers before attempting to acquire new customer tiers or expand acquisition channels.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Existing customer base with low repeat rate
no existing retention or subscription infrastructure
claims.mechanism: Each customer cohort acquired represents a compounding asset; implementing subscription and re-engagement cadence on existing customers multiplies revenue without the acquisition cost of new customers, creating the annuity base that makes further growth capital-efficient.
bounded_by: Assumes consumables have natural replenishment demand
Requires clear maintenance schedule or subscription trigger

examples.text: A duct cleaning supply distributor approached Alex Hormozi stating annual revenue of $1.2M and a desire to scale to $3.5M. When asked how he acquires customers, he responded 'strictly organic.' When asked if he can take more customers, he said 'yes.' Hormozi diagnosed this as representing solved product-market fit (good product, word-of-mouth validation, profitability) with an unsolved acquisition and retention problem. The business had never implemented systematic customer outreach, subscription offers, or consumable retention cadence. By implementing these without changing the product, the business could scale within the same customer pool and geographic reach.

The ink-and-printer business model works across three revenue wheels: hardware (printers, often sold at breakeven or loss), consumables (ink cartridges, 60-80% gross margin), and service contracts. The economic engine is not printer volume but installed-base size multiplied by consumable pricing and service retention. An auto dealership follows the same pattern: sell vehicles at low margin, monetize through service departments and parts sales at 70%+ margins. Duct cleaning supply mirrors this: sell equipment, monetize through consumables (cleaning compounds, filters) and service calls. In all three cases, manufacturer and distributor profitability depends on consumable and service capture, not hardware sales.

practices.text: For supply businesses with an existing customer base acquired through word-of-mouth, implement a re-engagement and subscription offer to existing customers before attempting to build new acquisition channels; offer consumables on a recurring cadence or subscription basis and communicate available products via outbound email or contact.

When scaling a service business built on equipment sales, treat the three revenue wheels (equipment, consumables, service) as distinct profit centers and establish target retention rates of 90-95% on consumables and service before expanding to new customer tiers or acquisition channels.

For B2B equipment supply businesses, make an explicit binary choice between outbound, paid ads, affiliates, or content-based customer acquisition and commit to that method with volume and consistency rather than attempting to optimize all four channels simultaneously.
